newsitem.title: NEPAL: Anti-tax strike shuts down Kathmandu business.
newsitem.headline: Anti-tax strike shuts down Kathmandu business.

text.p: A strike led by businessmen opposed to a proposed new tax brought commerce in the Nepali capital to a standstill on Monday, witnesses said.
Shops and businesses in Kathmandu were closed in response to the strike called by executives who oppose the government's plan to introduce a value added tax (VAT) later this year.
Last month the centre-left government announced in its 1997/98 budget proposal that it would introduce the VAT from November 16. Nepal's fiscal year begins in mid-July.
The new tax will replace the existing sales tax, which as part of the budget proposal was cut to 10 percent from 15, as well as taxes on contracts, hotels and entertainment.
The government has not yet specified the level of the VAT. Parliament is debating the budget proposal.
"Time is not ripe for the implementation of a value added tax," said Surendra Malakar, general secretary of the Nepal Chamber of Commerce which is heading the campaign against the new tax.
Businesses that register with the government will pay a 10 percent sales tax until the VAT takes effect, while unregistered firms will have to pay 20 percent.
"This is a way of forcing businessmen into the VAT net," Malakar told Reuters.
Opponents of the VAT say the government should take more time to study the VAT before introducing the new tax.
Businessmen are also demanding that the four-month old coalition government withdraw a measure proposed in the budget that would require a tax clearance certificate for any bank deposit over $8,810.

Businessmen said the provision would discourage investment and provoke a flight of capital from the fund-starved Himalayan kingdom. The government says the provision does not apply to current depositors.
